course.chapter_intro: Chapter {n} of Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (Sweigart, 2025), renewed for an advanced course.

playground.label: CSV to JSON to XML: one table, three formats (uses input)
playground.code:
import csv, json
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
raw = input('Rows (; between rows): ')
header, *data = csv.reader(raw.split(';'))
records = [dict(zip(header, row)) for row in data]
for record in records:
    record['qty'] = int(record['qty'])
print(json.dumps(records, indent=2))
root = ET.Element('fruits')
for record in records:
    item = ET.SubElement(root, 'fruit', name=record['fruit'])
    item.text = str(record['qty'])
ET.indent(root)
print(ET.tostring(root, encoding='unicode'))
back = json.loads(json.dumps(records))
print(back == records, type(back[0]['qty']).__name__, type(root[0].text).__name__)

findings: Chapter 18 of the 3rd edition teaches three plain-text formats for serialised data: CSV, read with csv.reader and written with csv.writer, with DictReader and DictWriter for files that carry a header row, and with a delimiter and a line terminator that can be changed to make tab-separated files; JSON, read with json.loads and written with json.dumps; and XML, read with xml.etree.ElementTree through fromstring, parse, iter and the tag and text attributes, and written with Element, SubElement, set and tostring. It closes with Project 13, which removes the header line from many CSV files, 11 practice questions and the practice program Excel-to-CSV Converter.

The chapter's printed behaviours reproduce under Python 3.14.4 when the book's own files are rebuilt: csv.reader gives a list of seven rows of strings for example3.csv and line_num runs from 1 to 7, a second pass over the same reader gives nothing, writerow returns 21, 32 and 16 for the three rows of the first writer example, 21, 30 and 16 for the tab-separated one and 16, 20, 15 and 20 for the DictWriter, json.dumps of the dictionary gives back the JSON text of the chapter character for character, and the XML iteration, filtering and tostring outputs match apart from the differences listed in the next finding.

Four printed outputs of the chapter do not reproduce as printed: the list shown for DictReader on exampleWithHeader3.csv has six dictionaries, but the file holds seven data rows and the first, for 4/5/2035 13:34 Apples 73, is missing from the printed list; the XML text in the chapter's interactive shell contains a typographic closing quotation mark after the namespace address, which the parser rejects as not well-formed at line 3, column 45, and the line breaks of the printed string put a newline into the street and the phone number; the printed tostring result writes the empty car element as /> while Python 3.14.4 writes ' />' with a space before the slash and moves the xmlns:xsi declaration to the root element when the text came from a parse; and the xmltodict output could not be run because the package is not installed in the interpreter used. The chapter also sends the reader to Chapter 18 for HTML although this is Chapter 18, while its other references name Chapter 13 for Beautiful Soup and CSS selectors.

The chapter says the line terminator of a CSV file is a newline by default, but the default of the excel dialect and of csv.writer is the two characters carriage return and line feed, which agrees with RFC 4180; this is why the files written by the chapter's examples hold '
' at the end of every row, why writerow counts 21 characters for a row of 19, and why the documentation says a file must be opened with newline='': on a system whose text layer turns '
' into '
', a file opened without it gets '
', which is the double spacing of the chapter's Figure 18-1. On this Linux system the file opened without newline='' came out right; the Windows behaviour was emulated with a text layer that translates the line feed and was not run on Windows.

Project 13 works as printed when run on three files in a temporary folder: it skips the file that does not end in .csv, writes the two others into headerRemoved without their first line and leaves the originals unchanged, although the introduction of the project says the old contents are replaced while the code writes to a new folder. Its test reader_obj.line_num == 1 finds the header only when the header is one line: the documentation says line_num counts lines read and not records, and a header with a newline inside a quoted name produced a first row whose line_num was 2, so the header stayed in the output; taking the first row with next() does not depend on the line count.

The chapter lists the Python values JSON can hold, and the documentation adds what happens at the edges: a tuple comes back as a list, the keys of a dictionary become strings so that loads(dumps(x)) == x fails for x = {1: 'a'}, a set or a date raises TypeError unless a default function is given, NaN and Infinity are written and read although the specification has no such numbers, a repeated name in an object keeps the last value, non-ASCII characters are escaped unless ensure_ascii is false, a byte order mark at the start raises ValueError, and a file should be opened with encoding='utf-8'.

For an advanced course, chapter 18 is best taught as a choice of format by the shape and the types of the data: CSV for rows with the same columns and only strings back, JSON for nested data with numbers, booleans and null kept, XML for documents with attributes, mixed text and namespaces, with every value text and null only by convention. The printed outputs hold under 3.14.4 except the four listed, and the course should add newline handling and the RFC 4180 terminator, the line_num hazard, the type limits of JSON, exception notes, the command-line tool, quoting modes, tomllib, incremental parsing and the XML security notes. Not executed: the practice program's use of openpyxl and xmltodict, because neither package is installed in the interpreter used, and any Windows behaviour.

Python 3.14 makes python -m json the preferred way to validate and pretty-print JSON, with python -m json.tool still working, and adds exception notes to JSON serialisation errors so that the source of the error can be identified, and the notes of an error for a set nested in a list in a dictionary name the dictionary keys and list items leading to it. Python 3.12 added QUOTE_STRINGS and QUOTE_NOTNULL to csv, so that None can be written unquoted and read back as None; Python 3.11 added tomllib, which reads TOML but has no writing function; since Python 3.12 testing the truth value of an Element emits a DeprecationWarning; and ET.indent, since 3.9, gives indented XML output.
title: CSV, JSON and XML files for an advanced course: chapter 18 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Delimited text
nodes.body: Delimited text is the chapter's first format: rows of cells separated by a character, read and written with the csv module (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Reading input
nodes.body: Reading a CSV file means making a reader from an open file and taking its rows (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Csv reader
nodes.body: csv.reader(example_file) takes the File object that open('example3.csv') returns and gives a reader, and list(reader) is a list of seven rows for the chapter's file; the function takes a file object or any iterable of lines, so csv.reader('ab,c') given a string reads the characters one by one and returns [['a'], ['b'], ['', ''], ['c']], while csv.reader(['ab,c']) gives [['ab', 'c']] (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: csv.reader takes a file object opened in text mode, or any iterable of lines, and gives an object that yields each row as a list of strings.

nodes.label: Rows and columns
nodes.body: After list(reader), example_data[0][0] is '4/5/2035 13:34', example_data[0][1] is 'Apples', example_data[1][1] is 'Cherries' and example_data[6][1] is 'Strawberries', the row index first and the column index second (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Converting the reader to a list gives a list of lists, so a cell is found by the row index and then the column index.

io.code:
(lambda csv, io: (lambda d: (d[0][0], d[0][1], d[1][1], d[2][2], len(d)))(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO('4/5/2035 13:34,Apples,73
4/5/2035 3:41,Cherries,85
4/6/2035 12:46,Pears,14
')))))(__import__('csv'), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: String values
nodes.body: A CSV file has no data types, so every cell comes back as a string: the three cells of '4/5/2035 13:34,Apples,73' are all of class str, the last plus '1' is '731' and int of it plus 1 is 74 (Sweigart, 2025); unquoted values become floats only when the reader is given quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Every cell comes back as a string, so a number in a file is converted by the program with int or float.

io.code: (lambda csv: (lambda row: ([type(v).__name__ for v in row], row[2] + '1', int(row[2]) + 1))(next(csv.reader(['4/5/2035 13:34,Apples,73']))))(__import__('csv'))

nodes.label: Line number
nodes.body: The reader's line_num starts at 1, so the chapter's loop prints Row #1 to Row #7 for the seven rows; the reader can be looped over once, and a second list() of the same reader gave 0 rows, so the file is opened again to read it again (Sweigart, 2025); line_num is the number of lines read and not the number of records, and a record that holds a line break inside quotes spans two lines, and the reader of '“a\nb”,c\nd,e' showed line_num 2 after its first record (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The reader's line_num counts the lines read so far, from 1, and a reader can be looped over once; line_num is not the number of records when a record spans lines.

io.code: (lambda csv: (lambda r: ([(r.line_num, row[1]) for row in r], len(list(r))))(csv.reader(['a,Apples', 'b,Cherries', 'c,Pears'])))(__import__('csv'))

nodes.label: Split versus reader
nodes.body: '“Hello, world!”,eggs'.split(',') gives ['“Hello', ' world!”', 'eggs'] and next(csv.reader(['“Hello, world!”,eggs'])) gives ['Hello, world!', 'eggs'], which is the pitfall the chapter names for splitting lines by hand (Sweigart, 2025) (Altis et al., 2003).
nodes.definition: Splitting a line at every comma cuts a quoted value that contains a comma in two, which the csv reader does not.

nodes.label: Writing rows output
nodes.body: Writing a CSV file means making a writer around a file opened for writing and giving it lists (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Csv writer
nodes.body: writerow(['spam', 'eggs', 'bacon', 'ham']) returns 21 for a row of 19 characters, because the line terminator of two characters is counted, and the chapter's three rows returned 21, 32 and 16 and produced the file text it prints, with the second row's first value in double quotes (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: csv.writer wraps a file object, and writerow writes one list as a row and returns the number of characters written, line terminator included.

nodes.label: Newline argument
nodes.body:
The chapter opens the output file with newline='' and says that on Windows a forgotten newline argument doubles the spacing (Sweigart, 2025); the documentation gives the mechanism, that a text layer with newline=None turns each '
' into the system's line separator while the csv writer already ends rows with '
' (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and emulated with a text layer that translates '
' to '
' the writer produced b'a,b
' where newline='' gave b'a,b
'; on this Linux system the file opened without newline='' held b'a,b
', and no run was made on Windows.
nodes.definition: A file given to the csv module is opened with newline='' so that the module's own line terminator is not translated a second time by the text layer.

io.code: (lambda csv, io: [(lambda b: (lambda t: (csv.writer(t).writerow(['a', 'b']), b.getvalue()))(io.TextIOWrapper(b, encoding='ascii', newline=n, write_through=True)))(io.BytesIO()) for n in ('', '\r\n')])(__import__('csv'), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: Quote escaping
nodes.body: Writing ['Hello, world!', 'say “hi”', 'x'] with a line feed as terminator gave '“Hello, world!”,“say ”“hi”“”,x' followed by a line feed, 31 characters: the value with a comma is quoted and the double quote inside the second value is doubled, as the chapter shows for the comma alone (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The writer puts a value in double quotes when it holds the delimiter, a double quote or a line break, and doubles any double quote inside it.

nodes.label: Tab separated
nodes.body: csv.writer(f, delimiter='\t', lineterminator='\n\n') wrote the chapter's three rows with tabs between cells and two line feeds after each row, and writerow returned 21, 30 and 16 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The delimiter and lineterminator keyword arguments change the character between cells and the characters at the end of a row, which makes a tab-separated file.

nodes.label: Header structure
nodes.body: A file with a header row is read and written as dictionaries whose keys are the column names (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Dict reader
nodes.body: csv.DictReader on exampleWithHeader3.csv gave seven dictionaries, the first {'Timestamp': '4/5/2035 13:34', 'Fruit': 'Apples', 'Quantity': '73'}, where the list printed in the chapter shows six and leaves out that first data row; the header row itself is not among the results, and the dictionaries are ordinary dict objects since Python 3.8 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: DictReader takes the first row as the keys and gives each later row as a dictionary, so the header row is not in the results.

nodes.label: Field names
nodes.body: DictReader on example3.csv, which has no header, used its first row as the keys and gave {'4/5/2035 13:34': '4/5/2035 3:41', 'Apples': 'Cherries', '73': '85'} as the first dictionary, and with ['time', 'name', 'amount'] as the second argument it gave seven dictionaries, the first for '4/5/2035 13:34' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: When a second argument gives the field names, DictReader uses them and treats the first row of the file as data.

nodes.label: Dict writer
nodes.body: csv.DictWriter(output_file, ['Name', 'Pet', 'Phone']) with writeheader and three writerow calls returned 16, 20, 15 and 20 and wrote the four lines the chapter prints; the order of the keys in each dictionary does not matter, only the order of the field names does (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: DictWriter takes the field names in the order the columns are to appear, writeheader writes them as the first row, and writerow takes a dictionary.

io.code: (lambda csv, io: (lambda s: (lambda w: (w.writeheader(), w.writerow({'Name': 'Alice', 'Pet': 'cat', 'Phone': '555-1234'}), w.writerow({'Phone': '555-5555', 'Name': 'Carol', 'Pet': 'dog'}), s.getvalue()))(csv.DictWriter(s, ['Name', 'Pet', 'Phone'], lineterminator='\n')))(io.StringIO()))(__import__('csv'), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: Missing keys
nodes.body: The row for {'Name': 'Bob', 'Phone': '555-9999'} is written as 'Bob,,555-9999', an empty cell for the missing 'Pet' (Sweigart, 2025); a dictionary with a key that is not a field name, {'a': 1, 'c': 3} for the fields a and b, raised ValueError: dict contains fields not in fieldnames: 'c', and with extrasaction='ignore' it wrote '1,' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A key missing from the dictionary becomes an empty cell, while a key that is not among the field names raises ValueError unless extrasaction is 'ignore'.

nodes.label: Csv format options
nodes.body: Options of the csv module that the chapter does not use decide quoting, detect a format and handle errors (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Quote modes
nodes.body: With quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC the row ['a', 1, 2.5] was written as '“a”,1,2.5' and read back with the same option as ['a', 1.0, 2.5], the numbers as floats; QUOTE_STRINGS of Python 3.12 wrote ['a', 1, None, ''] as '“a”,1,,“”' and read it back as ['a', 1.0, None, ''], so None survives, while the default writer wrote None as an empty cell that came back as '' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The quoting option decides which values are quoted on writing and how unquoted values are read back; QUOTE_NONNUMERIC reads unquoted values as floats, and QUOTE_STRINGS and QUOTE_NOTNULL of Python 3.12 let None survive.

io.code: (lambda csv, io: (lambda s: (csv.writer(s, quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, lineterminator='\n').writerow(['a', 1, 2.5]), s.getvalue(), list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(s.getvalue()), quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC))))(io.StringIO()))(__import__('csv'), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: Sniffer detection
nodes.body: The Sniffer of the csv module found the delimiter ';' in a sample 'a;b;c' with two rows of numbers and reported True for has_header on 'name,qty' above three rows such as 'x,1'; the documentation calls the header test a rough heuristic that can give false positives and false negatives (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The Sniffer guesses the delimiter of a sample of text and whether its first row is a header, as a rough heuristic that can be wrong.

nodes.label: Header project tool
nodes.body: Project 13 removes the first line from every CSV file in a folder and is written in three steps (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Header removal
nodes.body: Run on a.csv with 'h1,h2', '1,2' and '3,4', on b.csv and on a text file in a temporary folder, the chapter's program printed Removing header from a.csv... and Removing header from b.csv..., skipped the text file, wrote a.csv into headerRemoved as '1,2' and '3,4' with terminators '\r\n', and left the original a.csv unchanged; the project's introduction says the old contents are replaced, while the code writes a new copy into headerRemoved (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Project 13 reads each CSV file, skips the row whose line_num is 1 and writes the others to a file of the same name in a new folder.

io.code:
(lambda csv, io: (lambda r: [row for row in r if r.line_num != 1])(csv.reader(io.StringIO('Timestamp,Fruit
4/5/2035 13:34,Apples
4/6/2035 12:46,Pears
'))))(__import__('csv'), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: Multiline header hazard
nodes.body: For the text '“Time\nstamp”,Fruit' followed by one row, the test line_num != 1 kept all rows, including the header, because the header record is read with line_num 2; taking the header with next(reader) first gave only the data rows (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A header whose name holds a line break is one row over two lines, so the test line_num == 1 does not find it and the header is kept.

io.code:
(lambda csv, io: (lambda r: ([row for row in r if r.line_num != 1], r.line_num))(csv.reader(io.StringIO('\x22Time
stamp\x22,Fruit
x,y
'))))(__import__('csv'), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: Json data
nodes.body: JSON is the chapter's second format, for nested dictionaries and lists, read and written with the json module (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Json syntax rules
nodes.body: JSON text looks like a Python dictionary and list with a few changes (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Json values
nodes.body: json.dumps({'car': None, 'programmer': True, 'name': 'Alice Doe', 'age': 30}) gives '{“car”: null, “programmer”: true, “name”: “Alice Doe”, “age”: 30}': None is null, the booleans are true and false in lowercase, and the names are in double quotes (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: JSON writes missing as null and the two booleans as true and false in lowercase, with double-quoted strings and colons between names and values.

nodes.label: Json differences
nodes.body: A trailing comma in '[“spam”, “eggs”,]' raised JSONDecodeError: Illegal trailing comma before end of array at line 1 column 16, single quotes raised Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes, a comment after the value raised Extra data, and a line break inside a string raised Invalid control character, while json.loads('{“a”:\n  [1 , 2]}') gave {'a': [1, 2]}, so whitespace outside strings does not matter (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: JSON allows no trailing comma, no single quotes, no comments and no line break inside a string, and whitespace outside strings does not matter.

nodes.label: Json input
nodes.body: json.loads turns JSON text into Python values (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Loads function
nodes.body: json.loads of the chapter's JSON text gave the dictionary the chapter prints, with 'car': None and 'programmer': True, and the result is of class dict; json.load does the same from a file object, and a dumped and reloaded file compared equal to the data (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: json.loads takes a string of JSON text and returns the Python value, a dictionary for an object; json.load does the same for a file.

io.code: (lambda json: (lambda d: (d['name'], d['age'], d['car'], d['programmer'], type(d).__name__))(json.loads('{\x22name\x22: \x22Alice Doe\x22, \x22age\x22: 30, \x22car\x22: null, \x22programmer\x22: true}')))(__import__('json'))

nodes.label: Decode error
nodes.body: JSONDecodeError is a subclass of ValueError, its message gives the line and column of the fault, and JSONDecoder().raw_decode('[1, 2] extra') returned ([1, 2], 6), the value and the position where it ended (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Text that is not valid JSON raises JSONDecodeError, a kind of ValueError that carries the message and the line, column and character position of the fault.

nodes.label: Json output
nodes.body: json.dumps turns Python values into JSON text (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Dumps function
nodes.body: json.dumps of the chapter's dictionary returned the one-line text that json.loads had been given, equal to it character for character, and json.dumps(None) is 'null' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: json.dumps takes a Python value and returns the JSON text on one line; json.dump writes it to a file.

nodes.label: Indent option
nodes.body: indent=2 put the chapter's dictionary on 21 lines with two spaces per level and the same content as the chapter prints; an indent of '\t' used a tab per level, sort_keys=True ordered the names, and separators=(',', ':') gave the most compact text, '{“a”:2,“b”:1}' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The indent option puts each array item and each member on its own line, indented by that many spaces per level, or by a string such as a tab.

nodes.label: Json tool
nodes.body: echo '{“json”:“obj”}' | python -m json printed the object indented by four spaces and exited with 0, invalid input '{1.2:3.4}' printed Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1) and exited with 1, and python -m json.tool still ran; the What's New of 3.14 calls python -m json preferred to python -m json.tool and says the output is highlighted in color by default, which was not observed here because the output was piped (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Running the json module as a script checks JSON text from a file or standard input and prints it indented, or reports where it is invalid.

nodes.label: Json type conversion
nodes.body: JSON holds fewer types than Python, and the conversion changes some of them (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Type mapping
nodes.body: json.loads(json.dumps({'t': (1, 2), 'k': {1: 'a'}, 'f': 1.0, 'n': None})) returned {'t': [1, 2], 'k': {'1': 'a'}, 'f': 1.0, 'n': None}: the tuple became a list and the key 1 became '1', so json.loads(json.dumps({1: 'a'})) == {1: 'a'} is False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An object becomes a dict, an array a list, a number an int or a float; on the way out a tuple becomes an array and a dictionary key becomes a string, so the round trip does not always give back the original.

nodes.label: Unsupported types
nodes.body: json.dumps raised TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable for {1, 2}, the same for a date with its class name, and for the built-in open; the chapter lists strings, integers, floats, booleans, lists, dictionaries and None as the types JSON can store, and converting a set to a sorted list, json.dumps({'s': sorted({3, 1, 2})}), gave '{“s”: [1, 2, 3]}' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A value outside the basic types, such as a set, a date or a file object, raises TypeError when it is written, and is converted by the program first.

nodes.label: Default hook
nodes.body: json.dumps({'when': datetime.date(2035, 4, 5)}, default=str) gave '{“when”: “2035-04-05”}': the function given as default is called for the value JSON cannot write and its result is written instead (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The default argument names a function that JSON calls for a value it cannot write, and its result is written in place of the value.

nodes.label: Exception notes
nodes.body: json.dumps of {'k': [{'a': {1, 2}}]} raised TypeError with __notes__ equal to [“when serializing dict item 'a'”, 'when serializing list item 0', “when serializing dict item 'k'”], the path from the set outward, which Python 3.14 added (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Since Python 3.14 a TypeError from json.dumps carries notes that name the dictionary keys and list positions leading to the value that could not be written.

nodes.label: Xml data
nodes.body: XML is the chapter's third format, read and written with xml.etree.ElementTree (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Xml syntax rules
nodes.body: XML nests elements marked by tags, like HTML (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Elements and tags
nodes.body: Parsing '<person><name>Alice Doe</name><age>30</age></person>' gave a root with tag 'person', children with tags 'name' and 'age', and the text 'Alice Doe' and '30' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An XML element is a pair of tags with text or other elements between them; the elements inside an element are its children and it is their parent.

io.code: (lambda ET: (lambda r: (r.tag, [c.tag for c in r], r[0].text, r[1].text))(ET.fromstring('<person><name>Alice Doe</name><age>30</age></person>')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Single root
nodes.body: ET.fromstring of two person elements side by side raised ParseError: junk after document element: line 1, column 39, and one person element parsed to a root with tag 'person' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A valid XML document has one root element that holds all the others, so text with two elements side by side at the top is not valid.

nodes.label: Attributes versus elements
nodes.body: The address written as an element with attributes gave {'street': '100 Larkin St.', 'city': 'San Francisco'} as its attrib and no children, and written with a city child element it gave the text 'San Francisco' from find('city') and one child; the parser treats them differently, and the choice between them is left to the document (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The same data can be written as child elements or as attributes of one self-closing element, and nothing in XML decides which, so the choice is a convention of the document.

io.code: (lambda ET: (lambda a, b: (a.attrib, b.find('city').text, len(a), len(b)))(ET.fromstring('<address street=\x27100 Larkin St.\x27 city=\x27San Francisco\x27 />'), ET.fromstring('<address><city>San Francisco</city></address>')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Xml input
nodes.body: Reading XML means parsing the text to a root Element and walking the tree (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Parse functions
nodes.body: ET.fromstring('hi') returned a root with tag 'a', text 'hi' and attrib {'x': '1'}, and ET.parse of a file-like object returned an ElementTree of class ElementTree whose getroot() is the root, as ET.parse('my_data.xml') did for a file (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: ET.fromstring parses text and returns the root Element; ET.parse reads a file and returns an ElementTree, whose getroot gives the root Element.

io.code: (lambda ET, io: (lambda r, t: (r.tag, r.text, r.attrib, t.getroot().tag, type(t).__name__))(ET.fromstring('hi'), ET.parse(io.StringIO(''))))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']), __import__('io'))

nodes.label: Child access
nodes.body: For the chapter's person document, root.tag is 'person', list(root) gave the six children name, age, programmer, car, address and phone, root[0].text is 'Alice Doe', root[3].text == None is True, root[4][0].text is '100 Larkin St.', looping over root printed the six lines the chapter shows, root.iter() visited sixteen elements in document order and root.iter('number') printed the two phone numbers (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An Element is indexed like a list of its children, looped over for the children, and its iter method visits the element and all below it, optionally only those with one tag.

io.code:
(lambda ET: (lambda r: ([c.tag for c in r], [e.tag for e in r.iter()], [e.text for e in r.iter('number')]))(ET.fromstring('

A12

')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Find elements
nodes.body: On the documentation's country document, findall('country') gave the two names, find('country/rank').text gave '1', find('rank') on the root gave None because find looks only at children, and findall(“.//neighbor[@direction='W']”) gave ['Switzerland']; the path syntax is a small part of XPath (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: find and findall search the children by tag or by a small XPath path, and findall returns a list that is empty when nothing matches while find returns None.

io.code: (lambda ET: (lambda r: ([c.get('name') for c in r.findall('country')], r.find('country/rank').text, r.find('rank'), [n.get('name') for n in r.findall('.//neighbor[@direction=\x27W\x27]')]))(ET.fromstring('<data><country name=\x27Liechtenstein\x27><rank>1</rank><neighbor name=\x27Austria\x27 direction=\x27E\x27/><neighbor name=\x27Switzerland\x27 direction=\x27W\x27/></country><country name=\x27Panama\x27><rank>68</rank><neighbor name=\x27Colombia\x27 direction=\x27E\x27/></country></data>')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Xml output
nodes.body: Writing XML from Python builds an element tree and turns it into text (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Build elements
nodes.body: Building a root with Element('person'), a child with SubElement(person, 'name'), the text 'Alice Doe' and an attribute set('first', 'Alice') produced '<person><name first=“Alice”>Alice Doe</name></person>' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A document is built by making a root with Element and adding children with SubElement, setting text with the text attribute and attributes with set.

io.code: (lambda ET: (lambda p: (lambda n: (n.set('first', 'Alice'), n.__setattr__('text', 'Alice Doe'), ET.tostring(p, encoding='unicode'))[2])(ET.SubElement(p, 'name')))(ET.Element('person')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: To string bytes
nodes.body: ET.tostring(element) returned bytes, ET.tostring(element, encoding='unicode') returned a str, and for '' the bytes were b'', an empty element with a space before the slash, where the chapter prints it without the space; ET.indent(tree) of Python 3.9 gave the document on separate indented lines, and tree.write with xml_declaration=True put the declaration first (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: tostring returns bytes unless encoding='unicode' is given, which returns a string, and ET.indent adds line breaks and indentation before writing.

io.code: (lambda ET: (lambda e: (type(ET.tostring(e)).__name__, type(ET.tostring(e, encoding='unicode')).__name__, ET.tostring(e, encoding='utf-8')))(ET.fromstring('')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Xml processing tools
nodes.body: The chapter names two ways to read a large XML document and the modules that do it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Dom versus sax
nodes.body: xml.dom.minidom parsed '12' and gave ['1', '2'] for its b elements, xml.sax called a handler with start a, start b, text 1, end b, end a, and ET.iterparse gave the end events of b, b and a; the documentation of minidom advises those not proficient in the DOM to use ElementTree (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The DOM approach loads the whole document into memory and the SAX approach reads it as a stream of events, and ElementTree offers the tree plus iterparse for reading in steps.

nodes.label: Entity expansion
nodes.body: A 137-character document that defines three entities, each made of ten copies of the previous one, expanded to a text of 1000 characters in ET.fromstring; the documentation names the billion laughs and quadratic blowup attacks for Expat versions below 2.7.2, and the interpreter used reported expat_2.6.3, so data from outside must be treated as the XML security section says (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An XML document can define entities that the parser expands, so a short document can become a very large text; data from an untrusted source needs the precautions of the XML security section.

io.code: (lambda ET: (lambda x: (len(x), len(ET.fromstring(x).text)))('<!DOCTYPE l [<!ENTITY a \x270123456789\x27><!ENTITY b \x27&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;\x27><!ENTITY c \x27&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;\x27>]><r>&c;</r>'))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Xml text values
nodes.body: XML holds only text, and the program converts it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Text only values
nodes.body:
For '

30true

' the text of age is '30' and int of it plus 1 is 31, the text of programmer is the string 'true', the text of car is None, and its attribute is stored as '{http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance}nil' with the value 'true' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Every value in XML is text, a number or a boolean is converted by the program, and a missing value is only approximated with an xsi:nil attribute.

io.code:
(lambda ET: (lambda r: (r.find('age').text, r.find('programmer').text, r.find('car').text, r.find('car').get('{http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance}nil'), int(r.find('age').text) + 1))(ET.fromstring('

30true

')))(__import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Xml to dict
nodes.body: The chapter uses the third-party xmltodict.parse to get a dictionary from XML text; xmltodict is not installed in the interpreter used (importlib finds no such module), so its printed output was read from the chapter and NOT executed (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The third-party xmltodict turns XML text into nested dictionaries with @-prefixed keys for attributes, and leaves the values as text.

nodes.label: Format choice
nodes.body: Choosing between the formats rests on the shape of the data and on what comes back (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Format evaluation
nodes.body: The three formats give back different Python types for the same number (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Format comparison
nodes.body: The value 30 came back as a str from a CSV cell, as an int from json.loads('30') and as a str from the text of 30, so only JSON keeps the number (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The formats differ in what a value becomes on reading: CSV gives a string for every cell, JSON keeps numbers, booleans and null, and XML gives text.

io.code: (lambda csv, json, ET: [type(x).__name__ for x in (next(csv.reader(['30']))[0], json.loads('30'), ET.fromstring('30').text)])(__import__('csv'), __import__('json'), __import__('xml.etree.ElementTree', fromlist=['_']))

nodes.label: Toml reading
nodes.body:
tomllib.loads('name = “Alice Doe”
age = 30
programmer = true
') gave {'name': 'Alice Doe', 'age': 30, 'programmer': True}, tomllib has no dumps function, and a fault in 'a = ' raised TOMLDecodeError with the message Invalid value (at end of document), with lineno 1 and colno 5, attributes that Python 3.14 added to the exception; TOML reading was added in Python 3.11 (Hukkinen and Jain, 2022) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The standard library reads TOML with tomllib since Python 3.11 and has no function to write it; the chapter names TOML and YAML and leaves them out.

nodes.label: Exercise tools
nodes.body: The chapter ends with eleven practice questions and one practice program (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Exercise answers
nodes.body: The answers that code can show: csv.reader and csv.writer are given a File object, not a file name, for a reader the file is opened to read and for a writer to write with newline='', writerow takes a list, delimiter and lineterminator set the character between cells and the characters ending a row, all three formats are plain text that a text editor can edit, json.loads and json.dumps convert, XML is the format with tags in angle brackets, and JSON writes None as null and the booleans as true and false, as json.dumps(None) and json.dumps([True, False]) showed (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The eleven practice questions ask which features Excel has that CSV lacks, what the reader and writer take, and how JSON writes null and the booleans.

nodes.label: Excel to csv converter
nodes.body: The practice program reads Excel files with openpyxl and writes one CSV file per sheet; openpyxl is not installed in the interpreter used, so the workbook reading was NOT executed, and only the parts that do not need it were run: os.path.splitext('spam_data.xlsx')[0] is 'spam_data', the file names were spam_data_Sheet1.csv and spam_data_Totals.csv, and a stand-in sheet of lists written with csv.writer gave 'Fruit,Qty' and 'Apples,73' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The practice program writes one CSV file per sheet of each Excel file, named from the workbook name without its extension and the sheet title.
